q: Positive rays (canal rays) were discovered in 1886 by:
x: Goldstein used a discharge tube with a perforated cathode and saw rays passing through the holes behind it. Thomson studied cathode rays (electrons) and Chadwick discovered the neutron.

q: According to Planck's quantum theory, energy is emitted or absorbed:
o: Discontinuously, in small packets called quanta
Only by gases at high temperature
x: Planck proposed that radiant energy is emitted or absorbed in separate packets (quanta), not continuously. A quantum of light is called a photon.

q: An atomic orbital is best described as:
o: A fixed circular path of an electron around the nucleus
The total number of electrons in a shell
The region of space around the nucleus where the probability of finding an electron is maximum
The path followed by a photon
x: An orbital is a three-dimensional region of high electron probability. A fixed circular path is Bohr's orbit, an older idea.

q: The Aufbau principle states that electrons:
o: Must have opposite spins in every orbital
Fill orbitals in order of decreasing energy
Fill orbitals in order of increasing energy
x: Aufbau ('building up') means electrons enter the lowest-energy orbital available first. Opposite spins is Pauli's principle and filling degenerate orbitals singly is Hund's rule.

q: In Goldstein's discharge tube with a perforated cathode, the positive rays were observed:
o: Behind the cathode, after passing through its holes
Behind the anode, moving away from the cathode
Only at the surface of the anode
Only when a magnetic field was applied
x: Positive ions formed in the gas move towards the negative cathode; some pass through its holes and appear as a glow behind it. That is why they are also called canal rays.

q: In the equation E = hν, the value of Planck's constant h is:
x: h = 6.626 × 10⁻³⁴ J s. 6.022 × 10²³ is Avogadro's number, 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ is the electronic charge in coulombs and 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ is the electron's mass in kg.

q: The maximum number of electrons that one atomic orbital can hold is:
x: Each orbital holds at most two electrons, and they must have opposite spins (Pauli exclusion principle). Eight is the maximum for the second shell, not an orbital.

q: The Pauli exclusion principle states that:
o: Electrons fill the lowest energy orbitals first
Electrons pair up only after all degenerate orbitals have one electron
No two electrons in an atom can have the same set of four quantum numbers
The position and momentum of an electron cannot both be known
x: Pauli's principle means two electrons in the same orbital must differ in spin. The other statements are the Aufbau principle, Hund's rule and the uncertainty principle.

q: The e/m value of positive rays is highest when the discharge tube contains:
x: The H⁺ ion (a proton) is the lightest positive ion, so for the same charge it has the largest e/m. Heavier gases give heavier ions and smaller e/m values.

q: The energy of a photon is directly proportional to its:
x: E = hν, so energy rises in direct proportion to frequency. Since E = hc/λ, energy is inversely, not directly, proportional to wavelength.

q: Which statement correctly distinguishes an orbit from an orbital?
o: An orbit holds two electrons; an orbital holds 2n² electrons
An orbit is a definite circular path; an orbital is a region of probability
An orbital is a definite circular path; an orbit is a region of probability
They are two names for the same thing
x: Bohr's orbit is a fixed planar path at a fixed distance. An orbital, from wave mechanics, is a 3-D region where the electron is likely to be found.

q: Hund's rule states that electrons entering degenerate orbitals:
o: Occupy them singly with parallel spins before pairing begins
Pair up in the first orbital before the next is used
Always have opposite spins in separate orbitals
Enter the orbital of highest energy first
x: Electrons spread out one per orbital, with parallel spins, before any pairing occurs; this gives the most unpaired electrons and lower energy.

q: Which statement correctly contrasts positive rays with cathode rays?
o: Both have the same e/m whatever gas is used
The e/m of positive rays depends on the gas in the tube; that of cathode rays does not
Positive rays are much lighter than cathode ray particles
Cathode rays are deflected by fields but positive rays are not
x: Cathode rays are always electrons, so their e/m is constant. Positive rays are ions of whatever gas is present, so their mass and e/m change with the gas.

q: If the wavelength of a radiation is doubled, the energy of each of its photons becomes:
x: E = hc/λ, so energy is inversely proportional to wavelength. Doubling λ halves the energy of each photon.

q: The idea of a definite electron path was replaced by the orbital concept mainly because:
o: Electrons always move in straight lines
The nucleus is too small to be measured
The exact position and momentum of an electron cannot both be known at the same time
x: Heisenberg's uncertainty principle shows we cannot fix both the position and the momentum of an electron, so only the probability of finding it can be described. That probability region is the orbital.

q: The 4s subshell is filled before the 3d subshell because:
o: 4s has a higher principal quantum number
4s has a lower (n + l) value than 3d
4s is closer to the nucleus than 3d
x: For 4s, n + l = 4 + 0 = 4; for 3d, n + l = 3 + 2 = 5. The subshell with the lower n + l has lower energy and fills first.

q: Positive rays are produced in a discharge tube when:
o: Protons are emitted directly from the anode metal
Neutrons in the gas gain a positive charge
Electrons combine with gas molecules to form ions
Cathode ray electrons knock electrons out of gas molecules
x: Fast cathode rays collide with gas molecules and remove electrons, leaving positive ions; these ions form the positive rays. Gaining electrons would give negative ions, not positive rays.

q: Which of these radiations has photons of the highest energy?
x: X-rays have the highest frequency (shortest wavelength) of the four, and E = hν. Infrared has the lowest frequency, so the least energy per photon.

q: Orbitals of the same subshell that have equal energy, such as the three 2p orbitals, are called:
x: Orbitals of equal energy are degenerate. In a free atom the three p orbitals of a subshell are degenerate, as are the five d orbitals.

q: According to the (n + l) rule, when two subshells have the same (n + l) value, the one filled first is the one with the:
x: With equal n + l, the subshell with lower n has lower energy. For example 3d and 4p both have n + l = 5, and 3d fills first.

q: The mass of a proton is approximately:
x: A proton has a mass of 1.6726 × 10⁻²⁷ kg (1.6726 × 10⁻²⁴ g). 9.11 × 10⁻³¹ kg is the electron's mass and 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ is the size of the charge in coulombs.

q: A radiation has a frequency of 5 × 10¹⁴ Hz. Taking h = 6.6 × 10⁻³⁴ J s, the energy of one photon is:
x: E = hν = 6.6 × 10⁻³⁴ × 5 × 10¹⁴ = 33 × 10⁻²⁰ = 3.3 × 10⁻¹⁹ J. Dividing h by ν instead of multiplying gives 1.32 × 10⁻⁴⁸ J.

q: Cathode rays have the same charge-to-mass ratio (e/m) whatever gas is in the discharge tube and whatever metal the cathode is made of. This shows that:
o: Cathode rays are made of the gas atoms themselves
Electrons are a constituent of all atoms
Each element has its own kind of electron
x: Because identical particles come from every gas and every cathode, they must be common to all matter, so electrons are present in all atoms. The e/m of positive rays does depend on the gas, which is the contrast students mix up.

q: Millikan's oil-drop experiment measured:
o: The e/m ratio of positive rays
x: Millikan balanced charged oil drops in an electric field and found that every charge was a whole-number multiple of 1.602 × 10⁻¹⁹ C, the charge on one electron. The e/m of cathode rays was measured earlier by J. J. Thomson, which is the usual mix-up.

q: Chadwick discovered the neutron by bombarding beryllium with alpha particles: ⁹₄Be + ⁴₂He → X + ¹₀n. The nucleus X is:
x: Balance mass numbers: 9 + 4 = 13 = A + 1, so A = 12; balance atomic numbers: 4 + 2 = 6 = Z + 0, so Z = 6, carbon. Forgetting the neutron's mass of 1 gives ¹³C.

q: The e/m value of the electron is 1.76 × 10¹¹ C kg⁻¹ and its charge is 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C. The mass of an electron is:
x: m = e ÷ (e/m) = 1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹/1.76 × 10¹¹ = 0.909 × 10⁻³⁰ = 9.09 × 10⁻³¹ kg. Multiplying instead of dividing gives 2.82 × 10⁻⁸ kg, and dividing the other way round gives 1.10 × 10³⁰ kg.

q: Beams of electrons, protons, alpha particles and neutrons with the same speed pass through the same electric field. Arranged from most deflected to least deflected, they are:
x: Deflection depends on charge/mass. Taking the proton's charge and mass as 1: electron 1/(1/1836) ≈ 1836, proton 1/1 = 1, alpha 2/4 = 0.5, neutron 0 (no charge). Ranking by charge alone puts the alpha particle (charge 2+) above the proton, which is the trap.

q: Which species has 16 protons, 16 neutrons and 18 electrons?
x: 16 protons means sulphur; 16 neutrons gives mass number 32; 18 electrons means two more than the protons, a 2− charge: ³²S²⁻. ³⁴S²⁻ has 18 neutrons, and ³²S has only 16 electrons.

q: The radius of the first Bohr orbit of hydrogen is 0.529 Å. The radius of its third orbit is:
x: Bohr radius rₙ = 0.529 n² Å, so r₃ = 0.529 × 9 = 4.76 Å. Taking r proportional to n instead of n² gives 1.59 Å; 2.12 Å is the radius of the second orbit.

q: The energy of the electron in the nth orbit of a hydrogen atom is Eₙ = −1312/n² kJ mol⁻¹. The energy needed to remove the electron completely from the n = 2 orbit is:
x: E₂ = −1312/4 = −328 kJ mol⁻¹, and taking the electron to n = ∞ (energy 0) needs +328 kJ mol⁻¹. Dividing by n instead of n² gives 656; 984 kJ mol⁻¹ is the energy to move the electron from n = 1 to n = 2.

q: In the hydrogen spectrum, the line produced when an electron falls from n = 3 to n = 2 belongs to the:
o: Lyman series, in the ultraviolet region
Paschen series, in the infrared region
Balmer series, in the visible region
Balmer series, in the ultraviolet region
x: Lines are grouped by the lower level: transitions ending at n = 2 form the Balmer series, whose lines lie in the visible region (3 → 2 is the red line). Lyman lines end at n = 1 and lie in the ultraviolet; naming the series after the upper level (n = 3, Paschen) is the slip.

q: Using Eₙ = −1312/n² kJ mol⁻¹ for hydrogen, the energy given out per mole of photons when electrons fall from n = 3 to n = 2 is about:
x: ΔE = 1312(1/2² − 1/3²) = 1312 × 5/36 ≈ 182 kJ mol⁻¹; check: 328 − 145.8 = 182.2. Using only the energy of the n = 3 level gives 146, and using n = 1 to n = 3 gives 1166 kJ mol⁻¹.

q: In Rutherford's experiment, most alpha particles passed straight through a thin gold foil. This showed that:
o: Most of the atom is empty space
Electrons move in fixed circular orbits
The positive charge is spread evenly through the atom
x: Most particles met nothing to deflect them, so most of the atom's volume is empty; the few large deflections showed a tiny, dense, positive nucleus. Fixed electron orbits were Bohr's later idea, and an even spread of positive charge was the Thomson model that this result disproved.

q: How many orbitals are there in a subshell with azimuthal quantum number l = 2?
x: For l = 2, m takes the values −2, −1, 0, +1, +2, giving 5 orbitals (the d subshell). 10 is the number of electrons the subshell can hold, which is the usual mix-up.

q: The total number of orbitals in the shell with principal quantum number n = 4 is:
x: The shell has 4s, 4p, 4d and 4f subshells with 1 + 3 + 5 + 7 = 16 orbitals, which is n². 32 (2n²) is the maximum number of electrons, the tempting slip.

q: Which set of quantum numbers (n, l, m, s) is NOT allowed for an electron?
x: l can only take values from 0 to n − 1, so for n = 2 the largest l is 1; l = 2 is impossible. In the other sets l < n and m lies between −l and +l.

q: A 2pₓ orbital has two lobes along the x-axis. The nodal plane of this orbital, where the chance of finding the electron is zero, is the:
o: Plane at 45° between the x- and y-axes
x: The two lobes lie on either side of the nucleus along x, so the plane through the nucleus perpendicular to the x-axis, the yz plane, is the node. The xy and xz planes both contain the x-axis and cut through the lobes, which is the usual mistake.

q: The outermost (valence) electron of a potassium atom (Z = 19) in its ground state has the quantum numbers:
x: K is 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶ 4s¹; the 4s orbital fills before 3d because its (n + l) is smaller, so the last electron is 4s: n = 4, l = 0, m = 0. Expecting the 19th electron to go into 3d gives n = 3, l = 2.

q: The orientation of an orbital in space is described by the:
x: The magnetic quantum number m gives the orientation of an orbital, such as px, py or pz. The azimuthal quantum number l gives its shape (s, p, d, f), which is the usual mix-up; n gives size and energy, and s gives the spin.

q: The ground-state electronic configuration of calcium (Z = 20) is:
x: After argon (18 electrons) the next two go into 4s, which is lower in energy than 3d, giving [Ar] 4s². Putting them into 3d because 3 comes before 4 is the common slip.

q: The electronic configuration of the Fe²⁺ ion (Z of Fe = 26) is:
x: Fe is [Ar] 3d⁶ 4s²; when it forms an ion, the 4s electrons are lost first, giving [Ar] 3d⁶. Removing the last-filled 3d electrons instead gives [Ar] 3d⁴ 4s².

q: How many unpaired electrons are there in the Co²⁺ ion (Z of Co = 27) in its ground state?
x: Co is [Ar] 3d⁷ 4s²; Co²⁺ loses the two 4s electrons to give 3d⁷. By Hund's rule the five d orbitals hold one electron each, then two of them pair: 7 − 2 × 2 = 3 unpaired. Taking all seven d electrons as unpaired forgets that pairing must start once each of the five d orbitals holds one electron.

q: Which ground-state configuration breaks Hund's rule?
x: Hund's rule says electrons occupy degenerate orbitals singly, with parallel spins, before pairing. Carbon's two 2p electrons should be 2px¹ 2py¹; pairing them in 2px while 2py is empty breaks the rule. Oxygen and fluorine must pair because they have more than three 2p electrons.

q: In a ground-state iron atom (Z = 26), how many electrons have the azimuthal quantum number l = 1?
x: Fe is 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² 3p⁶ 3d⁶ 4s². Electrons with l = 1 are in p subshells: 2p⁶ + 3p⁶ = 12. Counting only one p subshell gives 6; adding the 3d⁶ electrons (l = 2) gives 18.

q: A period 4 element in its ground state has one electron in the 4s subshell and a completely filled 3d subshell. Its atomic number is:
x: [Ar] 3d¹⁰ 4s¹ has 18 + 10 + 1 = 29 electrons: copper, whose filled 3d¹⁰ is more stable than 3d⁹ 4s². Chromium (24) is also 4s¹ but has a half-filled 3d⁵; zinc (30) has 4s², and potassium (19) has no 3d electrons.
